title: EBIT and Operating Income
subtitle: Earnings before interest and tax - measuring pure operating efficiency
openingQuestion: Why is EBIT more useful than Net Income when comparing two companies with different debt structures?
openingOptions: Net Income isn't a standardised metric
EBIT is always larger than Net Income
EBIT strips out the effect of interest and tax - it measures operations alone
explanation: EBIT = Revenue − COGS − OpEx, stopping right before interest and tax. Those two items say nothing about whether a company runs its business well: interest depends on how much debt management chose to take on, and tax depends on where it's registered and what incentives apply. Cutting them out leaves exactly the part generated by the business - which is why a heavily indebted company can be placed next to a debt-free one and still compared fairly.

diagram.label: Revenue minus cost of goods and operating expense
Stop right before interest and tax
That gives EBIT: the part generated by the business
This is what makes two differently-leveraged companies comparable

realWorldExample.description: Hoa Phat is a good example for understanding EBIT in a capital-intensive industry. The group takes on large debt to invest in integrated steel complexes (such as Dung Quat), leaving it with sizeable annual interest expense. Comparing Hoa Phat with a less-leveraged steel peer using Net Income alone would understate Hoa Phat's real operating efficiency, since most of the gap comes from interest expense rather than production performance - which is exactly why EBIT/Operating Margin is a fairer yardstick for comparing companies with different amounts of financial leverage.

quiz.question: What is EBIT?
options: Net profit left after subtracting all interest and tax owed for the reporting period
EBIT = Earnings Before Interest & Tax - operating profit before interest and tax
The cash a company generates from operations during the reporting period
The company's total operating cost before calculating tax
quiz.explanation: EBIT = Operating Income. Two names for the same thing. It shows pure business efficiency.

quiz.question: How does EBIT differ from Net Income?
options: EBIT is always larger than Net Income because it also includes all financial income
Net Income is always larger than EBIT because a tax refund is added back
EBIT hasn't subtracted interest and tax yet; Net Income has subtracted both
The two metrics are identical, just different names used across standards
quiz.explanation: EBIT reflects business operations. Net reflects the final profit for shareholders after every cost.

quiz.question: A company has negative net income but positive EBIT. What's the cause?
options: An accounting error - if EBIT is positive, Net Income can't be negative
That can't happen - the two metrics always share the same sign
The company booked revenue it hasn't yet collected, turning profit negative
Interest and tax are so high that Net Income turns negative even though EBIT is positive
quiz.explanation: EBIT = 100, Interest = 150 → Net = -50. This can happen if the company carries too much debt.

quiz.question: What is EBIT Margin?
options: EBIT / Revenue - pure operating efficiency, equal to Operating Margin
EBIT / Total Assets - the return earned on all assets
Gross Profit / Revenue - the gross profit left per dong of revenue
EBIT / Shareholders' Equity - operating profit per dong of paid-in equity
quiz.explanation: EBIT Margin = EBIT / Revenue. An EBIT Margin of 15% means every 100 of revenue produces 15 of operating profit.

quiz.question: Company A: Revenue 1000, EBIT 200. EBIT Margin = ?
options: 200% (= 1,000/200 turned into a percentage)
50% (= 200/400, the gross profit portion)
Cannot be calculated without knowing COGS

quiz.question: To compare the operations of two companies with different interest expense and tax structures, what should you use?
options: Net Income, since it's the final figure after every cost has been subtracted
Revenue, since revenue isn't affected by capital structure
EBIT or EBITDA - they strip out the effect of interest and tax
Gross Profit, since it sits above both interest and operating expense
quiz.explanation: EBIT is clean because it removes everything unrelated to core business operations.

quiz.question: What is the difference between EBITDA and EBIT?
options: EBIT adds D&A back while EBITDA leaves depreciation expense as-is
EBITDA has subtracted tax while EBIT hasn't subtracted tax owed yet
The two metrics are the same, EBITDA is just an American term for it
EBITDA adds D&A back; EBIT still counts depreciation as an expense
quiz.explanation: EBITDA = EBIT + D&A. Used to compare companies when D&A differs (because their asset bases differ).

quiz.question: A company sells more but EBIT falls. What could be the cause?
options: COGS grew faster than revenue, or operating costs increased
An accounting error, since selling more should always raise EBIT
Interest expense rose, since interest is subtracted before reaching EBIT
The tax rate rose, cutting the company's operating profit
quiz.explanation: EBIT = Revenue - COGS - OpEx. If it falls while Revenue rises, COGS or OpEx grew too fast.

quiz.question: What do investors care about most in EBIT?
options: The absolute value of EBIT - the bigger the number, the better the company
EBIT Margin and its trend - whether operations are improving
Only whether EBIT is positive or negative - the magnitude matters little
It doesn't matter much, since EBIT doesn't yet reflect shareholder profit
quiz.explanation: Absolute EBIT means little without knowing the margin. An EBIT Margin of 5% versus 15% tells very different stories.

quiz.question: Which important ratio is EBIT used to calculate?
options: Gross Margin = EBIT divided by the company's total net revenue for the current reporting period
It's only used to forecast revenue for the next period
Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT / Interest Expense - the ability to pay interest
None - EBIT is only ever presented, never used in a ratio
quiz.explanation: ICR = EBIT / Interest Expense. Banks look at ICR to decide whether to extend a loan.

quiz.question: Companies A and B have the same EBIT, but A carries far more debt than B. Is comparing their EBIT fairer than comparing their Net Income?
options: No, because Net Income is always the best metric for comparison
Yes - EBIT removes the effect of their different capital structures
No, because EBIT doesn't reflect real operating efficiency
Neither EBIT nor Net Income can be used to compare them
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why EBIT exists: by ignoring interest and tax - two factors driven by financing decisions rather than operating efficiency - EBIT provides a level playing field for comparing companies with different capital structures.

keyTakeaways: EBIT measures operating efficiency, independent of capital structure
EBITDA = EBIT + D&A - a proxy for cash generation

practicePrompt.question: Company A carries heavy debt (100 billion/year in interest), Company B carries almost none (5 billion/year in interest). Both have the same EBIT of 300 billion. If you only look at Net Income, which company looks 'less operationally efficient', and is that a fair conclusion?
options: A has lower Net Income because of interest, but equal EBIT means the operations run just as well
Company A is definitely operating less efficiently than Company B, since its final Net Income will be much lower
The two companies can't be compared at all because they carry different amounts of interest expense
Company B is always better than Company A in every respect because it carries less debt
practicePrompt.explanation: EBIT measures operating efficiency independent of capital structure, because it's calculated before subtracting interest and tax. Two companies with equal EBIT (300 billion) are running their core businesses equally efficiently, even though their Net Income differs because of a difference in debt levels (capital structure), not because of the business itself.

summary.keyIdea: EBIT measures operating efficiency, independent of capital structure
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: EBITDA = EBIT + D&A - a proxy for cash generation

application.title: Calculate EBIT and Operating Margin yourself
application.message: From a company's financial statements, calculate EBIT = Revenue − COGS − OpEx and Operating Margin = EBIT/Revenue yourself, then compare it with a peer in the same industry to see who runs a more efficient operation.
application.secondary: Comparing within the same industry is the fair way, since each industry has its own typical margin level.

sections.text: If you want to compare two companies in the same industry where one carries heavy debt and the other almost none, Net Income will mislead you. EBIT is the tool for comparing apples with apples.
What EBIT is and why it's neutral to capital structure

EBIT (Earnings Before Interest and Tax - usually equivalent to Operating Income) = Revenue − COGS − Operating Expenses. Because this calculation stops before subtracting interest and tax, it purely reflects a business's ability to generate profit from its core operations, unaffected by whether the company chose to finance itself with debt or equity, or what tax rate it faces.
Operating Margin: a measure of core efficiency

Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue shows how much operating profit each dong of revenue generates. This is analysts' preferred metric for comparing companies in the same industry with different debt structures, since it filters out the distortion caused by financial leverage.
EBITDA: one more step removing non-cash cost

EBITDA = EBIT + Depreciation & Amortization (D&A). Depreciation and amortisation are non-cash accounting charges reflecting the spreading of fixed/intangible asset value over many years. By adding D&A back, EBITDA sits closer to the cash actually generated by operations, and is especially useful for comparing companies with very different levels of fixed-asset investment (CapEx), such as a telecom company versus a software company.

items: EBIT = Gross Profit − SG&A − R&D (equivalent to Operating Income).
Operating Margin = EBIT / Revenue - compares operating efficiency across companies.
EBITDA = EBIT + D&A - sits closer to actual operating cash flow.
Don't use EBITDA as a full substitute for cash-flow analysis - even though non-cash, D&A still reflects the need to reinvest in assets in the future.

left.label: Use EBIT when
left.text: Comparing operating efficiency across companies with different capital structures (debt/equity) within the same industry.

right.label: Use EBITDA when
right.text: Comparing companies with very different levels of fixed-asset investment and depreciation, for example infrastructure, telecom, or heavy manufacturing.
